questions.q: The quadratic $f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$ with $a > 0$ is minimised at...
questions.why: Setting $f'(x) = 2ax + b$ to zero gives the vertex. With $a < 0$ the same point is a maximum.

questions.q: A twice-differentiable function is convex exactly when...
options: Its Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere
questions.why: The second-order condition is the standard test. A convex function can have no minimum (for example $e^x$) or many (a flat region).

questions.q: For a separable function $f(x) = \sum_i f_i(x_i)$, how can you find its minimum?
options: By minimising the sum of the $x_i$
Only by gradient descent on all coordinates jointly
questions.why: Without interaction terms, each coordinate's optimum doesn't depend on the others.

questions.q: At a critical point, the Hessian has eigenvalues $3, 0, 1$. What can you conclude?
options: The second-order test is inconclusive because of the zero eigenvalue
It is a strict local minimum
questions.why: A zero eigenvalue means the quadratic model is flat in that direction, so higher-order terms decide. If all were positive it would be a strict minimum.

questions.q: Is the intersection of two convex sets convex?
options: Only if they overlap in a single point
questions.why: If two points lie in both sets, the segment between them lies in each set, hence in both. The union of convex sets usually isn't convex.

questions.q: A point $x$ lies inside the polytope $\{x : Ax \le b\}$ when...
options: At least one row is satisfied
questions.why: A polytope is an intersection of half-spaces, so every constraint must hold. Points with some equality lie on the boundary.

questions.q: Which function is convex on all of $\mathbb R$?
questions.why: Softplus has second derivative $\sigma(x)(1 - \sigma(x)) > 0$. $x^3$ is convex only for $x \ge 0$.

questions.q: Why does convexity matter for optimisation?
options: Every local minimum is a global minimum
Gradient descent converges in one step
questions.why: For a convex function, any point where no small move improves the value is globally optimal, so local methods are enough.

questions.q: Gradient descent on $f(x) = 5x^2$ with step size 0.3 does what?
questions.why: The update is $x \leftarrow (1 - \eta f'')x$ with $f'' = 10$. A step below $2/10 = 0.2$ is needed; between 0.1 and 0.2 it converges while oscillating.

questions.q: What distinguishes stochastic gradient descent from batch gradient descent?
options: It adds noise to the parameters
Each update uses the gradient of one (or a few) examples instead of the full dataset
It uses a random learning rate
questions.why: Mini-batch gradients are noisy but cheap and unbiased estimates of the full gradient, so you get many more updates per epoch.

questions.q: With momentum $v \leftarrow \beta v + g$, $\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta v$, and a constant gradient $g$, what is the eventual step size?
questions.why: The velocity converges to $g/(1 - \beta)$; with $\beta = 0.9$ steps are 10 times larger in consistent directions, while oscillating components partly cancel.

questions.q: How does Nesterov momentum differ from classical momentum?
options: It evaluates the gradient at the look-ahead point $\theta - \eta\beta v$
questions.why: Looking ahead lets the update correct for where momentum is about to carry it, which reduces overshoot and improves the convex convergence rate.

questions.q: Doubling the batch size halves what, roughly?
options: The variance of the gradient estimate
questions.why: Averaging twice as many independent examples halves the variance. The expected gradient is the same.

questions.q: The loss curve oscillates wildly and occasionally spikes. Which change is most likely to help first?
options: Remove momentum entirely and raise the learning rate
questions.why: Large oscillations usually mean the step size is near or above the stability limit for the sharpest directions.

questions.q: In SGD, why shuffle the data each epoch?
options: To avoid correlated consecutive batches that bias the updates
It is needed for momentum to work
questions.why: Ordered data (for example sorted by label) gives a sequence of biased gradients. Shuffling keeps each mini-batch a fair sample.

questions.q: Gradient descent on a quadratic bowl with condition number 100 and the best fixed step size converges at roughly what rate per step?
options: The error shrinks by $1/\kappa$ per step
questions.why: With the optimal step $2/(\lambda_{min} + \lambda_{max})$, the contraction factor is $(\kappa - 1)/(\kappa + 1)$, so about 115 steps per factor of 10.

questions.q: AdaGrad divides by $\sqrt{\sum_t g_t^2}$. What is its main weakness on long training runs?
options: The accumulated sum only grows, so the effective learning rate decays towards zero
It is not invariant to the learning rate
questions.why: AdaGrad suits convex and sparse problems but stalls in deep learning. RMSProp replaces the sum with an exponential moving average.

questions.q: RMSProp keeps $v \leftarrow \rho v + (1 - \rho)g^2$. What does dividing by $\sqrt v$ achieve?
options: Each parameter's step is normalised by its recent gradient magnitude
It projects the gradient onto a sphere
questions.why: Parameters with consistently large gradients take smaller steps and those with small gradients take larger ones, which helps in narrow valleys like Rosenbrock's.

questions.q: Adam's update magnitude per parameter is roughly bounded by...
options: The learning rate, regardless of the gradient's scale
questions.why: $\hat m/\sqrt{\hat v}$ is about $\pm1$ when gradients are consistent, so the step is about $\eta$. That scale invariance is why Adam needs less learning-rate tuning across layers.

questions.q: What is the difference between Adam with L2 regularisation and AdamW?
options: AdamW applies weight decay directly to the weights, not through the adaptive gradient
questions.why: With L2 added to the gradient, Adam's normalisation shrinks the decay for parameters with large gradients. Decoupling makes the decay uniform, which generalises better in practice.

questions.q: Adam's bias correction matters most when?
options: In the first steps, because $m$ and $v$ start at zero
When the learning rate is large
questions.why: The correction factors $1 - \beta^t$ approach 1 quickly for $\beta_1 = 0.9$ (after about 50 steps) and more slowly for $\beta_2 = 0.999$.

questions.q: Logistic regression trained with Adam versus plain gradient descent: which is guaranteed to reach the same minimum?
options: Both can reach the unique minimum for a strictly convex loss, given suitable step sizes
questions.why: Strict convexity gives one minimum; both methods can converge to it, although Adam with a fixed learning rate may hover around it without decay.

questions.q: What role does $\epsilon$ play in $\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,\hat m/(\sqrt{\hat v} + \epsilon)$?
options: It prevents division by zero and caps the step for parameters with tiny gradients
questions.why: When $\hat v$ is near 0, $\epsilon$ dominates the denominator, so steps stay bounded. Larger values make Adam behave more like SGD with momentum.

questions.q: Which optimiser keeps the most state per parameter?
questions.why: Adam stores $m$ and $v$, so its optimiser memory is twice the parameter size (in full precision). That matters for large models.

questions.q: Why use linear warmup at the start of training?
options: Early gradients and Adam statistics are unreliable, so large steps can destabilise training
It is required by the cosine schedule
questions.why: Warmup lets the second-moment estimates settle and avoids early divergence, which is common in transformers with large learning rates.

questions.q: A cosine schedule from $\eta_{max}$ to 0 over $T$ steps has what value at $t = T/2$?
questions.why: $\eta_t = \frac{\eta_{max}}{2}(1 + \cos(\pi t/T))$, and $\cos(\pi/2) = 0$.

questions.q: What do warm restarts (SGDR) do?
options: Periodically reset the learning rate to a high value and anneal again
Reset the optimiser state each epoch
Increase the batch size over time
Restart training from the initial weights
questions.why: Each cycle anneals to a low learning rate, then jumps back up, which can escape sharp regions and gives snapshots at each cycle end.

questions.q: In an LR range test, the loss is recorded while the learning rate grows exponentially. How do you pick the maximum learning rate?
options: At the largest learning rate tested
At the learning rate with the lowest loss exactly
Somewhat below the point where the loss starts to rise sharply
At the very start of the test
questions.why: The loss falls fastest well before divergence. A common heuristic picks a value a factor of a few below the blow-up point.

questions.q: A one-cycle schedule does what?
options: Ramps the learning rate up to a maximum and then down to well below the start
Decays the learning rate exponentially from the start
questions.why: The high-rate middle phase explores, and the long anneal at the end settles. Momentum is often cycled in the opposite direction.

questions.q: Sweeping learning rates over a grid, which spacing is usual?
questions.why: Good learning rates span orders of magnitude, so a log grid covers the range with few points.

questions.q: Training with a constant learning rate ends with the loss hovering above its minimum. Why does decaying the learning rate help?
options: SGD noise keeps the iterate bouncing; smaller steps shrink that noise ball
questions.why: With a fixed step, stochastic gradients keep the parameters in a region whose size scales with the step. Annealing lets them settle.

questions.q: Linear warmup for 1,000 steps to $\eta_{max} = 3\times10^{-4}$: what is the learning rate at step 250?
questions.why: Linear warmup gives $\eta_{max}\cdot t/T_{warm} = 3\times10^{-4}\cdot0.25$.

questions.q: ISTA for the lasso alternates a gradient step with which operation?
questions.why: Soft-thresholding is the proximal operator of $\lambda\|w\|_1$. It shrinks coefficients and sets small ones exactly to zero.

questions.q: You accumulate gradients over 4 micro-batches of different numbers of real (unpadded) tokens. How should you combine them to match one big batch?
options: Sum the per-token loss gradients and divide by the total token count across all micro-batches
Average each micro-batch's mean loss equally
questions.why: Averaging per-micro-batch means gives tokens in small micro-batches more weight than tokens in large ones. Normalising by the global count reproduces the single-batch gradient.

questions.q: Inverted dropout scales kept activations by $1/(1 - p)$ during training. Why?
options: So the expected activation is unchanged and no scaling is needed at test time
questions.why: Each unit survives with probability $1 - p$; dividing by that keeps its mean equal to the full network's.

questions.q: Early stopping with patience 5 means what?
options: Stop when validation loss hasn't improved for 5 consecutive evaluations, and restore the best checkpoint
Stop when training loss rises 5 times
questions.why: Restoring the best checkpoint matters; the last weights are by construction worse than the best by up to 5 evaluations.

questions.q: L1 regularisation tends to produce sparse weights, while L2 doesn't. Why?
options: L2 adds noise to the weights
L1's penalty has a constant slope near zero, so small weights are pushed all the way to zero
questions.why: L2's gradient $2\lambda w$ vanishes as $w \to 0$, so weights shrink but rarely reach exactly zero.

questions.q: Which data leak most commonly inflates validation accuracy?
options: Fitting preprocessing (scalers, vocabularies, imputation) on all data before splitting
questions.why: Statistics computed on the validation set leak its distribution into training. Fit preprocessing on the training split only.

questions.q: Validation loss rises while training loss keeps falling. What is happening?
options: The learning rate is too small
questions.why: The model is fitting noise specific to the training set. Regularisation, more data or early stopping help.

questions.q: Weight decay with coefficient $\lambda$ in plain SGD multiplies the weights by what each step, before the gradient update?
questions.why: Adding $\lambda w$ to the gradient gives $w - \eta(g + \lambda w) = (1 - \eta\lambda)w - \eta g$. For SGD this matches L2 regularisation with penalty $\frac\lambda2\|w\|^2$.

questions.q: Newton's method for logistic regression converges in few iterations because...
options: It uses a larger learning rate
Near the optimum it converges quadratically, using the curvature
questions.why: Each step solves a weighted least-squares problem (IRLS). The cost is a $d\times d$ solve per iteration, fine for small $d$.

questions.q: What is the cost of forming and inverting the Hessian for $d$ parameters?
questions.why: For a model with $10^9$ parameters that is impossible, which is why deep learning uses first-order methods or cheap curvature approximations.

questions.q: L-BFGS approximates the inverse Hessian using what?
options: The last $m$ pairs of parameter and gradient differences
The full Hessian computed every $m$ steps
The diagonal of the Hessian only
questions.why: It never forms a matrix: a two-loop recursion applies the approximation to the gradient in $O(md)$ time.

questions.q: Clipping gradients **by value** (each component to $[-c, c]$) differs from clipping by global norm how?
options: It can change the gradient's direction
questions.why: Components above $c$ are capped while others aren't, so the vector rotates. Global-norm clipping rescales uniformly and keeps the direction.

questions.q: Why can Newton's method move towards a saddle point in non-convex problems?
options: It only works on convex functions and stops elsewhere
Its step size is too small
It always follows the negative gradient
It jumps to the critical point of the local quadratic model, which may be a saddle
questions.why: With negative Hessian eigenvalues, $-H^{-1}g$ points uphill in those directions. Damping or saddle-free variants address this.

questions.q: Adaptive gradient clipping scales a layer's gradient based on what?
options: The ratio of the gradient norm to the parameter norm for that layer
questions.why: Clipping relative to the weight's own size keeps the relative update bounded, which made training normaliser-free networks stable.

questions.q: On an ill-conditioned quadratic bowl, which optimiser typically needs the fewest steps?
options: Newton's method (one step on an exact quadratic)
SGD with a tiny learning rate
questions.why: Newton's step uses the exact Hessian, so it lands on the minimum of a quadratic immediately. Adaptive and momentum methods sit in between.

questions.q: A loss spike appears and then recovers. Which mechanism is designed to limit the damage from rare huge gradients?
questions.why: Clipping caps the size of any single update, so one bad batch can't throw the parameters far away.
